title: TB1-14614
frame:
Forum: Refugee Protection Division (first-instance tribunal).
Parties: the claimant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review: none; this is the first-instance decision.
How the layers nest here: The member of the tribunal is the author (layer 1). The claimant and the Minister make submissions to the member (layer 2). There is no earlier decision-maker unless the reasons describe a prior decision (layer 3). Testimony and documents are layer 5.

paragraphs.text: The principal claimant, XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX (PC), his spouse, XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, (female claimant) their son, XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX (minor claimant) and the female claimant's brother, XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX (TC) all citizens of Guatemala, seek refugee protection pursuant to sections 96 and 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act1 (IRPA). The claimants' identities have been established through certified copies of passports and birth certificates.2 The PC was appointed Designated Representative of the minor claimant.

The claimants began supporting the Patriota Party (PP) in 2007 by handing out promotional materials and attending meetings. In XXXX 2008, the PC received threatening phone calls telling him to stop their political activities. On XXXX XXXX, 2008, the claimants were ambushed by armed men when they were on their way to a political meeting where Otto Perez Molina, the leader of the PP was speaking. The PC, the female claimant, the TC and another individual who was with them was beaten and the female claimant was told she would be next if they did not stop their political activity. Passersby came to their aid and took them to a hospital however the PC's parents arrived and took them to their family doctor for treatment. The TC left Guatemala City to live with his mother in a small village six hours away. He left Guatemala in XXXX 2008. The PC, female claimant and minor claimant went to live with the PC's parents in another zone in Guatemala City where they remained living until the PC's departure to the United States (U.S.) in XXXX 2009 and the female's and minor claimant's departure nine months later in XXXX 2009. The precipitating incident that caused the female and minor claimant to leave was an attempting kidnapping on XXXX XXXX, 2009. All claimants remained in the U.S. until their arrival at the U.S./Canada border in 2011.

I find that the claimants have not satisfied the burden of establishing a serious possibility of persecution for a Convention ground, or that they would personally be subjected, on a balance of probabilities, to a danger of torture, or a risk to life, or a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment, upon return to Guatemala. Therefore, I find that the claimants are neither Convention refugees, nor persons in need of protection pursuant to sections 96 and 97(1) of the IRPA.

The determinative issue in this claim is whether the claimants' fear of persecution due to political opinion is well founded. Having reviewed the evidence in its entirety, I find that it is not. Background

At the time that the claimants began their political activity in 2007 there was an election taking place which resulted in the UAE Party winning and President Colon taking office in January 2008. The country conditions state that the PP who also won seats were blocking bills presented to the Congress which understandably was not viewed favorably by those who supported the UNE. Since the claimants' departure from Guatemala. the PP, which the claimants supported were elected as government. No Objective Basis
Having reviewed the evidence in its entirety, I find that the claimants' political activities were minimal. They comprised of attending meetings and handing out promotional materials.

The documentary evidence indicates that there was a Presidential election on November 9, 2007 during which more than 40 were killed preceding the vote. A second round of voting took place on November 4, 2007 which resulted in the Unidad Nacional de la Esparanza (UNE) Party winning with 53% of the vote. President Colon took office in January 2008. It is in this context that the incidents leading to the departures of the TC in XXXX 2008, the PC in XXXX 2009 and then the female and minor claimants in XXXX 2009.

The PC and female claimant were attracted by the PP's platform to deal with delinquents and increased crime. According to statements made in their narratives the PC began to receive death threats on January 7, 2008, a few days after the UNE took office. Given this is the first time that the claimants experienced any problems due to their political activity, I find that their activity leading up to the November 9, 2007 election day and subsequent round of voting on November 4, 2007 was minimal.

The claimants' evidence is that the PC and TC were beaten by unknown persons on XXXX XXXX, 2008 when they were travelling to a speech that Otto Perez Molina was giving in XXXX. They have provided documents to show that this incident took place which includes statements taken by a police officer, XXXX XXXX XXXX which described the PC, female claimant and TC being ambushed by heavy armed men with bullet-proof vests who forced them to stop their vehicles and told them as to stop campaigning in the west as it was their territory.3 I assign no weight to this evidence as they are simply statements on paper that has no official police letterhead or police stamps to show that they were completed by a police official. In addition they provided two documents which are statements from the family doctor at their request regarding treatment they received on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2008: i) C-5 pages 8 and 9 is a medical certificate requested by TC on XXXX XXXX, 2008 with a reference number of XXXX from a doctor XXXX XXXX, a surgeon, which states: "That today he provided assistance in urgent consultation to Mr. XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, 33, being in serious conditions as he manifested having being unconscious for several minutes..."4 ii) C-7 pages 15 and 16 is a medical certificate from the same doctor dated on the same date of XXXX XXXX XXXX 2008 with a reference number of XXXX which states, "That today I provided assistance to Mr. XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, 26, ...who is consulting for lesions caused to him two months ago. The traumatism has disappeared with the local treatment and anti-inflammatories along with respiratory exercises. The immobilizer cast was removed and therapy was ordered for his complete recovery."5

Given that both the PC and TC were beaten and treated on the same day, and by the same doctor, it is puzzling why the certificates reference numbers are not in sequence but more troubling is this doctor refers to having treated the PC two months earlier for lesions and that the visit was to remove a cast. Of further concern is a third medical certificate, dated XXXX XXXX XXXX 2009 which is the same format as the above two medical certificates, and is signed by the very same doctor in which he states that he saw the female claimant for anxiety caused by the attempted kidnapping of her son, which according to the narrative happened on XXXX XXXX, 2009. The doctor states that the certificate was provided, "At the request of the interested party and for any legal effects I issue the present certification in this city of Guatemala, on XXXX XXXX, 2009." I find it questionable that the reference number which appears on this document has the reference number of XXXX which sequentially follows that of XXXX which is the reference number that appears on the medical certificate provided for the PC which was requested on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2008, some 19 months earlier.

Although this concern was not put to the claimants at the hearing, I am unable to find that these medical certificates provide reliable evidence to show that the PC was treated for injuries related to the XXXX XXXX XXXX 2008 incident wherein he was beaten by armed individuals as alleged in his narrative. Further, given sequential numbering, I find it implausible that the very next certificate completed by this doctor 19 months after treating the PC would relate to the female claimant. Consequently, this provides reason to assign no weight to statements made by this doctor to corroborate the kidnapping incident of XXXX XXXX, 2009.

Even if I accept that the claimants were involved in an incident in XXXX 2008 the evidence indicates that after this incident in XXXX 2008, the TC relocated to another area, 6 hours from Guatemala City and the PC and his family moved in with his parents in another district of Guatemala City where they allege they continued receiving death threats even though they were no longer active.

The claimants have provided four statutory declarations from persons who state that people have been asking for them. One is from a neighbor where the claimants lived previous to moving with the PC's parents which is dated May 25, 2012,6 and three other statutory declarations were from the PC's parents.7 I assign no weight to the 3 statutory declarations completed in 2012 as I do not find them trustworthy given that each of these sworn declarations, completed on three separate dates in 2012, are comprised of two pages, the second of which is identical in content, including a signature from the same lawyer/notary and identical notary stamps. Further, these second pages with the notary's signature are identical when placed one on top of the other which lead me to conclude they are photocopies of the same page. I therefore cannot assign them any weight, and draw negative inference against allegations made by the claimants that anyone was looking for them. The earlier statutory declaration provided by the PC's parents which is dated October 20, 2011 is also notarized by the same lawyer/notary. This document also is comprised of two pages. The content on the first page begins one third down on the page which would be reasonable if there was letterhead of the lawyer/notary however this area of the page is blank. The result of the content beginning so far down the page results in the need for a second page which while it appears to have been notarized by the same lawyer given the signature appears similar, the notary stamp is very different from that which appears in the above 3 declarations from the same notary. Given that this is a separate page from that which contains the statements as signed by the PC's, and the absence of any initials by the notary to show that it relates to that which was being notarized, it is not clear whether this second page was notarizing the attached statements or someone else's. Further, the lawyer/notary stated immediately above her signature that the incidents described in the declaration occurred in 2008 however the kidnapping incident according to the claimant's narrative and testimony happened on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2009. For these reasons I assign no weight to this earlier statutory declaration.

The claimants have provided other reports8 from persons who reported having gunshots fired at their home at some point in 2011 after they had been threatened by phone to stop their political activities. These reports do not indicate what party these persons were supporting; for example, were they the same as the claimants? It would appear given the reports are dated XXXX XXXX XXXX 2011 and XXXX XXXX, 2011 that the incidents happened during the latest election. While this corroborates evidence appearing in country condition documents provided by counsel and that contained in the NDP speak to election related violence in Guatemala during the 2011 elections, the evidence in large part discusses poorly enforced campaign oversight laws which create a prime environment for criminal groups looking to build up influence.9 Indeed, evidence appearing in counsel's documents detail political violence during the general election of September 11 and security forces arresting persons linked to crime including a candidate running for mayor for allegedly being involved in the murder of at least two political opponents to the general election of September 11 and simulating an attack against himself.10 Other evidence provided by counsel indicates that a deputy minister and his brother were murdered; however, these murders were being investigated by the National Police and the newly inaugurated President Molina reiterated that investigations in that case will continue because "we will not leave the crime unpunished."11 While other evidence12 provided by counsel indicates that a PP member was killed at her place of business, I am unable to find that the claimants before me fit the profiles of these above persons who actively sought political office during elections. These claimants had minimal political activity. They stopped their political activities in 2008. I do not find it credible that anyone, would be interested in them as they have alleged in their narratives and documents which state that unknown persons are looking for them.

Documentation shows that on November 6, Otto Perez Molina of the PP won a four-year term as president. The OAS international observation mission characterized the elections as generally free and fair. The Office of the Human Rights Ombudsman reported 36 killings of political activists or candidates, mostly at the municipal level, during the election cycle. There were few arrests or convictions for such killings, and the actors behind them were generally unknown.

While I accept that there is political violence in Guatemala, particularly during elections and that many of those who run for political office or have significant political activity have been killed, as stated above, this is not the profile of these claimants.

Having reviewed the evidence in its entirety, I can accept that the claimants' minimal support of the PP and limited political involvement made them nervous for their safety particularly when leaders or active PP members were subject to violence. I was not persuaded by the evidence that the XXXX 2008 theft of the PC's vehicle or the XXXX 2009 kidnapping incident were due to perceived political opinion but on balance acts of random violence by criminals. I find that allegations of telephone threats at their home or the PC's parent's home after they moved there are not credible. The PC provided evidence which he alleges in a police report in which he states that he received threats however this evidence has no probative value as the document has no official police letterhead or stamps to show that this is an official police document.

Country condition documents13 indicate that violent crime in Guatemala has not decreased since the claimants' departures to the United States and subsequent arrival to Canada in 2011, including politically motivated crime. The evidence indicates that the government under President Molina has continued to employ the military to support police units in response to rising crime particularly in Guatemala City's high-crime neighborhoods and other areas due to increased crime and gang activity.

There are several theories in circulation that attempt to explain the emergence of gangs in Guatemala and other Central American countries. Some analysts claim that the most notorious gang - Mara Salvatrucha or MS-13 - originated in El Salvador over three decades ago and their membership spread to neighboring Guatemala and Honduras. Another account calls the birth of Guatemalan Maras a by-product of an urban youth protest movement that first appeared in Guatemala City in the 1960s in response to social injustices and government abuses, and became increasingly violent in the mid-1980s when the clashes with police became common along with looting and bus-burning. One of the more widely accepted explanations traces the origins of gangs in Guatemala back to the wars that seized Central America in the 1970s and 1980s. Many Guatemalans and other Central Americans fled to the United States to escape the turmoil. Many of the children of these immigrants encountered a thriving gang culture and, for various reasons, joined these gangs. When the Central American wars began to wane in the early to mid-1990s, the United States deported thousands of convicted, jailed gang members to Central America at the end of their sentences. These deportees found themselves suddenly forced to eke out a new life in a country that was nearly or completely foreign to them. Jobless and, in many cases, unable to speak Spanish, these returnees began to replicate the social structure and economic base that had served them well in the United States - the gang. They set up new gangs in Guatemala and other Central American countries, which have now evolved into their own particular strains, though many have maintained strong links to gangs in the United States.

Similar to other countries in the region, estimates of the number of gang members in Guatemala vary widely, ranging from 14,000 to 165,000. According to the National Civilian Police, there are 340 maras in Guatemala and the localities with the greatest gang presence are Zones 6, 7, 12, 18, and 21 in Guatemala City, along with Villa Nueva, Mixco, and Amatitlan on the periphery. The two largest youth gangs in Guatemala are the Mara Salvatrucha 13 (MS-13) gang, with members comprising approximately 80 percent of the total number of gang members in the country, and 18th Street (Barrio 18), whose members comprise about 15 percent, and the remaining five percent making up other smaller, copycat gangs.

Gangs and gang members in Guatemala are not homogenous.14 There is no single typology applicable to every gang or gang member. Not all gangs have the same objectives, nor do they engage in the same type of activity or with the same degree of violence. Gang structures in Guatemala are not static. Gangs appear to have a very strong adaptive capacity and are able to readily evolve to changing political, economic, and social contexts.

The documentary evidence further indicates that societal violence is rampant, actors including gangs, committed numerous killings during the year.15 Gangs have now grown into a transnational criminal hydra involved in murder, extortion, and some gun and drug smuggling. Unfortunately, poor data collection systems make an accurate measure of gang membership difficult, but there are between 14,000 and 165,000 members in Guatemala.16 Gangs attack and extort money primarily from buses and small businesses17 and have become more violent and are often involved in extortion of neighbourhood residents, businesses, and public transportation operators, as well as in neighbourhood drug dealing.18 While all segments of the population have suffered, some professions are targeted more frequently, including private security guards, bus drivers and businesses.

The fact that a person or group of people may be victimized repeatedly or more frequently by criminals, for example, because of their perceived wealth or because they live in a more dangerous area19 or that they continue to be pursued after reporting to police or relocating,20 does not remove the risk from the exception if it is one faced generally by others. Thus, the consequential harm faced in these circumstances does not mean that the risk is not a generalized one.21

As stated above, the documentary evidence before the Board indicates that Guatemala is a democracy, and there are free and fair elections. There is a relatively independent and impartial judiciary. There is persuasive evidence that indicates that Guatemala candidly acknowledges its past problems, and is making serious efforts to rectify the corruption and impunity that exists. The Board accepts that Guatemala is experiencing challenges in addressing the criminality and also corruption that exist within the security forces in Guatemala. The Board recognizes that there are some inconsistencies among several sources within the documentary evidence; however, the preponderance of the objective evidence regarding current country conditions suggests that, although not perfect, there is an adequate state protection in Guatemala and that Guatemala is making serious efforts to address the problem of criminality, and that the police are both willing and able to protect victims.

Although the documentary evidence for Guatemala shows that there exists some level of tolerance by the police for some of the illegal groups in Guatemala in certain situations, and that those who actively support political parties are at risk, I find that there is insufficient evidence to indicate that this would be the case for these particular claimants. I find there is insufficient evidence to support counsel's assertion that the claimants would be at a heightened risk because of their minimal political activity in 2007 and 2008. They been away from Guatemala for 3 years and their political party is now in office. On balance, I find that the claimants fear is one of generalized risk which in part explains their not having sought protection in the U.S. during their 2 year stay in that country which is inconsistent with a subjective fear due to political opinion.

Consequently, I find that there is insufficient evidence before me that the claimants would face persecution or, on a balance of probabilities, face a risk to his life, or a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment, or a danger of torture, if they returned to Guatemala. For all these reasons, I find that that the claimants are neither Convention refugees nor persons in need of protection, whether under section 96 or section 97 of the IRPA.
Therefore, I find that the claimants are neither Convention refugees pursuant to section 96 of the IRPA, nor persons in need of protection pursuant to sections 97(1)(a) and 97(1)(b) of the IRPA.

Accordingly, the Refugee Protection Division rejects these claims for refugee protection.
